extracted.intended_audience: news industry professionals (editors, executives, product and data teams), policymakers, and researchers interested in AI and journalism
extracted.subtask_description: A research-informed set of evaluative considerations and criteria for how news organizations adopt, deploy, govern, and assess AI across editorial, commercial, and technical domains — and the implications for the public arena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives for adopting AI
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary motivations for adopting AI can be grouped into four broad categories: (i) technological developments, (ii) market pressures, (iii) industry dynamics, and (iv) uncertainty, hype, and hope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether AI adoption is being driven by clear strategic objectives (e.g., efficiency, new business models, product innovation) versus mere hype or competitive anxiety. Beware of adoption motivated chiefly by ‘what others are doing’ without a clear plan for value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate task selection / use-case fit
rubrics_metrics.description: AI is applied across a range of tasks (access and observation; selection and filtering; processing and editing; publishing and distribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match AI tools to tasks where they add value (e.g., transcription, fuzzy-matching in large document sets, dynamic paywalls, personalization) and avoid assuming suitability for tasks that require human judgment. Use the Table 2 categories (information discovery, verification, categorization, transcription, content production, personalization, etc.) as a checklist of candidate domains and test suitability empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context- and task-dependent efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential efficiency gains from AI are task- and context-dependent and can be curtailed by unreliable outputs, reputational risks, and the difficulty of automating certain tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess efficiency claims on a per-task basis with real-world metrics (time saved, conversion lift, accuracy). Examples: transcription often yields large time savings; dynamic paywalls may boost conversion; fuzzy matching can enable investigative work otherwise infeasible. Beware overgeneralizing from single examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human oversight and journalist autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Currently, AI aids news workers rather than replaces them, but AI use risks undercutting journalists’ autonomy by limiting discretionary decision-making abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain human-in-the-loop processes for editorial judgment, verification, and final sign-off. Evaluate workflows for points where AI could silently shift decision-making from journalists to algorithms and introduce safeguards to preserve editorial control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and explainability of AI systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The lack of transparency in AI systems raises worries about biases or errors creeping into journalistic output, especially as generative AI models gain prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand transparency from vendors about training data, model limits, and failure modes. Prefer tools with explainability features and document how outputs are produced. Use transparency as a criterion when choosing third-party providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependency on platform companies / lock-in risk
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations make extensive use of AI products and infrastructure from major tech companies, creating lock-in effects that limit autonomy and increase vulnerability to price changes and shifting platform priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the trade-offs between convenience/cost-effectiveness of platform AI and the long-term risk of dependency. Consider multi-vendor strategies, open-source alternatives, or building in-house capabilities where feasible to avoid single-vendor lock-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sharing and model training risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever news organizations provide access to archives, allow scraping, or use platform AI on their data, they risk improving platforms’ models — potentially strengthening competitors or enabling platforms to supplant journalistic roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize contract terms about data use; pursue explicit opt-outs where possible; evaluate the downstream impacts of giving platforms access to proprietary or archival datasets. Treat data-sharing decisions as strategic bargaining points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opt-out and vendor default settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Some AI services (e.g., AWS AI services) by default use customer content to train the vendor’s models; opting out can be possible but not straightforward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess vendor default data-use settings and the practical feasibility of opting out. Include data-governance checks in procurement and vendor onboarding processes to prevent inadvertent model training using proprietary content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity and resource disparities among publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Larger, better-resourced news organizations are more likely to build in-house AI, while smaller publishers often rely on third-party platform solutions, reinforcing existing inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating AI strategies, consider organizational capacity: talent, compute, datasets, and negotiation leverage. Incorporate measures to support smaller/local publishers (e.g., consortiums, shared infrastructure) to avoid widening gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on the public arena and gatekeeping role
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations shape the public arena as gatekeepers — changes to newswork via AI will alter the information ecosystem and the availability of accurate, accessible, diverse, relevant, and timely independent information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate AI deployments not only by internal metrics but by their broader effects on public information quality, diversity of voices, and democratic functions. Use public-interest criteria when deciding where to deploy AI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory, ethical, and reputational constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation, professional norms, resistance from news workers, audience preferences, and incompatible technical infrastructures act as constraints on AI adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include legal compliance, ethical review, staff consultations, and audience testing in rollout plans. Anticipate regulation and integrate compliance and ethical safeguards from the outset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not assuming AI frees journalists for better work
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not a given that AI will free up journalists to do deeper or better journalism; time savings may be immediately filled with new demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design process changes intentionally: if the aim is to reallocate saved time to deeper reporting, codify and protect that reallocation rather than assuming it will happen organically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for governance frameworks balancing innovation and harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing frameworks to balance innovation through AI in the news with concerns like copyright and various forms of harms will remain a difficult but necessary task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create cross-functional governance (editorial, legal, product, data, ethics) to assess use cases, foreseeable harms, copyright implications, and mitigation strategies. Engage with external standards and industry initiatives where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based evaluation of AI tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about AI benefits (e.g., conversion lift, time savings) are often cited but can be difficult to verify; empirical evidence is needed to substantiate effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require pilots, A/B tests, and measurable KPIs (conversion rates, time saved, accuracy rates) before widespread adoption. Document results and share learning across the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting journalistic quality and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreliable AI outputs risk reputational damage; accuracy and trustworthiness remain central to journalistic missions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institute verification steps for AI-generated or AI-assisted content, require editorial review, and be transparent about corrections. Prioritize accuracy over speed when AI outputs are uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiating terms with platform companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers that can invest in R&D and build infrastructure are in a stronger position to demand better terms when negotiating with platforms and technology companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat commercial agreements and data-access deals as strategic assets. Smaller organizations should seek collective bargaining, licensing models, or alternative partnerships to secure fair terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarding against inadvertently improving competitor AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Using platform AI services or allowing scraping can help platforms build better general-purpose AI products that might later perform tasks central to journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the competitive implications of contributing data or usage signals to platform providers. Where necessary, restrict data flows or negotiate clauses that prevent training on proprietary content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of audience experience and attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform AI-enhanced search experiences, short-answer formats, or AI-curated summaries may reduce visibility of full news content and change audience engagement patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how AI-enabled products affect long-form content consumption, audience retention, and civic information needs. Monitor shifts in engagement and adapt editorial/product strategies to preserve depth where valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and inclusive benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Some AI applications (e.g., text-to-speech, transcription) provide clear accessibility benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize AI use cases that improve accessibility and inclusion (transcription, translation, audio), and measure impact on audiences who benefit from these features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for upfront costs and organizational change
rubrics_metrics.description: AI adoption incurs early costs, requires organizational and strategic changes, and demands investment in talent and infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for initial costs, change management, training, and long-term maintenance. Set realistic timelines for when productivity gains can be expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure and traceability of AI-generated content
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions arise about whether we should be able to tell if a human or AI wrote a story and in which context disclosure is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop policies for disclosing AI involvement in content creation, with clear thresholds for when disclosure is required (e.g., wholly AI-generated pieces, automated summaries). Keep audit trails for AI-assisted editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of defining AI and focusing on capabilities rather than semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no consensus on what constitutes AI; for practical purposes in newsrooms, focus on what systems do (narrow, weak AI that simulates human activities in narrowly defined domains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define AI operationally for procurement and editorial policies (e.g., the report’s definition: computationally simulating human activities in narrowly defined domains) to avoid semantic disputes and ensure consistent governance.
